title: Edge case walkthrough — context lengths, TPS spikes & streaming resiliency
summary: SE-led walkthrough focusing on a set of edge cases: very long-context sessions, bursty high TPS, streaming backpressure interactions with proxies/timeouts, and recommended config and fallback patterns. Agreed to run a short benchmark and share a tuning checklist + sample prompts. Action items assigned for security doc handoff and pilot timeline.
topics: high TPS burst handling and autoscale

transcript:
Meeting header: 2025-03-18 16:32 PDT / Duration ~62m / Recording auto-started
Attendees: Liam Chen (Redwood AE), Marisol Rivera (Redwood SE), Jon Park (Product), Aisha Qureshi (Nimbus CTO), Tom Becker (Nimbus ML Eng), Priya Malhotra (Platform), Evan Ross (SRE)

Summary (auto): walkthrough of long context + high TPS + streaming failure modes, demo of Console suggestions and Optimize recommendations.

[00:00] Liam (AE): okay hey everyone thanks for joining, uh let's do quick intros — Liam on the AE side, Marisol our solutions engineer, Jon from product — and then Aisha and team — thanks for carving out the time.
[00:16] Aisha (CTO): yeah hi all — excited to see how Redwood behaves under our workloads, we push long user histories and we have bursty spikes during sync windows.
[00:28] Marisol (SE): great, we'll focus on three cases — very long context sessions, high TPS spikes (short bursts), and streaming backpressure + timeouts. We'll also show Console and Optimize suggestions.
[00:44] Tom (ML Eng): quick note — our current stack is a mix of hosted endpoints and an internal cache tier; most requests are 3–6k tokens but we have threads that can go up to 40k and sometimes longer for transcripts.
[00:58] Marisol (SE): got it, ok so first long context: Redwood's runtime supports variable context strategies — prefix caching, rolling KV cache, and in Console you can pin model variants that have different memory/kv profiles. For >32k contexts we recommend sharding the prompt and using the prefix cache to avoid repeated recomputation.
[01:18] Evan (SRE): when you say prefix cache, are we talking about a per-customer KV stored on GPU memory or offloaded? we've seen memory evictions cause OOMs in other systems.
[01:28] Marisol (SE): good question — we maintain an LRU-ish prefix store in GPU-backed memory with tiering to host RAM; if the active set exceeds capacity we fall back to a quantized variant or an offload to host RAM, that can add 20–80ms depending on sequence length. Not perfect but predictable.
[01:45] Tom (ML Eng): okay, so if we have many concurrent users with long histories, how does batching interact? won't batching wait for tokens and increase tail latency for real-time flows?
[01:58] Marisol (SE): yes batching is a trade-off — Console/Optimize can set per-route policies: low-latency routes disable batching, high-throughput routes allow adaptive batching. The runtime does continuous batching with a max-wait cap to bound tail latencies. We usually show configs where the max-wait is 8–12ms for low-latency.
[02:17] Aisha (CTO): can you demo that? maybe start with a high-concurrency test.
[02:22] Marisol (SE): sure, pulling up the Console… (typing) ok Route configs: here's one labeled 'interactive' low-latency, batching disabled, prefix-cache enabled; and here's 'ingest-batch' high-throughput, batching enabled 64ms window, max batch size 128.
[02:41] Jon (Product): note — Optimize will analyze your past token distribution and suggest an ideal batch window and quantization profile, it's not purely manual.
[02:50] Liam (AE): quick aside — on model fallback, if a high-capacity model is unavailable we can route to a quantized variant with similar semantics but lower memory—customers often prefer that to outright failures.
[03:02] Evan (SRE): streaming backpressure — our infra has an NGINX reverse-proxy that sometimes kills idle connections after 60s; if Redwood streams tokens slowly because of a long KV repair, do you see broken streams?
[03:18] Marisol (SE): yes proxies are the usual culprit — streaming is chunked transfer encoding and we recommend keepalive + shorter idle timeouts upstream. Also implement client-side streaming buffer with application-level heartbeats.
[03:34] Tom (ML Eng): in our tests with other providers we've seen sockets stall and then client retries duplicate items. Do you provide idempotency or resume tokens for streams?
[03:45] Marisol (SE): we surface chunk sequence IDs in the streaming API and the client SDK has a resume token pattern — if a connection drops you can request missing offsets. It's not perfect if chunks are dropped by proxies, but it helps.
[04:02] Aisha (CTO): what's the recommended client timeout then? we currently have 30s.
[04:07] Marisol (SE): for long-response streaming set client timeout bigger than your expected long tail—e.g., 3–5 minutes for transcript consolidation. For interactive messages aim for 60–90s. And have an exponential backoff retry with jitter.
[04:22] Evan (SRE): we worry about retries leading to doubled cost during spikes. Any way to do cheap early failures?
[04:29] Marisol (SE): yes use rate-limiting headers and a circuit-breaker: Redwood will return an HTTP 429 with Retry-After. Also Console can set per-route throttles and shed load to a cheaper fallback model or a cached answer.
[04:43] Tom (ML Eng): demo the high TPS waveform — perhaps burst to 5k RPS for 30s and see autoscale?
[04:50] Marisol (SE): we can simulate — I'm launching a script on our internal bench to produce 5k request/s to the 'ingest-batch' route (note: in the recording this is a simulated dedicated pool).
[05:12] [SFX: typing and a brief pause as load starts]
[05:20] Marisol (SE): load started — metrics showing queue size spike, autoscaler kicked a burst capacity lane, latency median stays about 45ms, p95 rises to 320ms briefly then back to 120ms after warm-up.
[05:38] Tom (ML Eng): that's not bad. what's the cost delta when you spin burst lanes?
[05:43] Liam (AE): depends on instance type and minutes used — Console shows an estimated cost increase in real-time; Optimize will recommend a cheaper quantized model or recommend more aggressive prefix-cache to reduce tokens computed. We'll send a cost-per-minute estimate in the follow-up.
[05:57] Aisha (CTO): what about timeouts at the HTTP layer during this spike, do you surface a difference between server-side timeouts vs client side?
[06:05] Marisol (SE): yes we instrument both — if a server-side worker times out you'll see a 502 or 504 with a trace id; client-side timeouts are logged as client aborts. We record both and map them in Console.
[06:18] Evan (SRE): in case of 504 from our reverse proxy, is there a way to preserve partial output? currently partial chunks are discarded.
[06:27] Marisol (SE): we can ship chunk ids and a small resumable artifact; we also advise using the SDK's persistent websocket mode which does a better job at resumption.
[06:40] [00:06:45] Tom (ML Eng): question on tokenization — our transcripts sometimes have weird token blow-ups with certain unicode characters, can quantization or a token-stitching preprocessor help?
[06:55] Marisol (SE): tokenization is model-specific; Optimize will flag token outliers and recommend pre-tokenization cleaning or a detokenization step. We also support a prompt-compaction service that canonicalizes repeated phrases to reduce token count — it's optional and lossy but useful for transcripts.
[07:13] Jon (Product): jumping in — another edge-case we see is long-running sessions where KV cache grows and causes GC pauses, we instrumented per-tenant cache quotas to prevent single tenant from blowing up a node.
[07:27] Aisha (CTO): do you have any sample configs for per-tenant throttles and eviction policies?
[07:33] Marisol (SE): yes, in Console under 'Advanced -> Tenant quotas' you can set max-kv-entries, eviction-policy = lru|lfu, and a soft-guarantee threshold. We can export an example config after the call.
[07:49] Evan (SRE): streaming backpressure again — sometimes the runtime will slow token emission when the GPU is doing KV swap; how do you signal upstream to slow client write rates?
[07:58] Marisol (SE): we provide flow-control hints via the streaming protocol (X-Flow-Window headers) so a client can adjust read buffer sizes; sadly not all proxies preserve such headers, so we put fallback heuristics in the SDK.
[08:15] Tom (ML Eng): let's talk errors — say a worker gets preempted mid-generation, what's the best pattern to avoid duplicate completions?
[08:24] Marisol (SE): two patterns: optimistic dedupe with generation ids (client includes request id; server attaches sequence) and server-side transactional checkpoints for long runs. The latter is heavier but helps for very long regenerations.
[08:38] Aisha (CTO): can Redwood do a canary fallback? e.g., route 10% to quantized model automatically if p95 latency > threshold?
[08:47] Jon (Product): yes — Console supports rollout policies by SLO. You can set p95 latency threshold -> automatic fallback ratio and also a hard failover to last-known-good commit.
[08:58] Marisol (SE): demoing Optimize quickly — here it ingests sample traces and suggests three profiles: "low-latency interactive", "balanced", and "cost-optimized". For Nimbus it suggests balanced with 8ms batch window, mixed int8 quantization, and prefix cache size 2x current.
[09:19] [SFX: brief screen share of Console, graphs moving]
[09:32] Tom (ML Eng): can Optimize estimate token-level cost savings for changing quantization? we've seen non-linear quality drops.
[09:39] Marisol (SE): it gives a projected token-cost delta and a quality delta score derived from eval sets; we recommend running an eval harness with your prompts. We'll share a sample harness.
[09:51] Evan (SRE): for our security/compliance we need audit logs of who accessed what prompts and outputs — is that retained in Private mode?
[09:59] Liam (AE): yes Private (VPC) gives you control plane logs + audit retention options and you can integrate with your KMS. We'll attach the SOC2 / network diagram.
[10:10] Aisha (CTO): fine, let's schedule a short pilot — what do you need from us to start?
[10:15] Liam (AE): sample prompt set, an expected TPS profile (burst shape + duration), and any SRE constraints (proxy timeouts). We'll run a 1-hour pilot on a dedicated pool and share metrics.
[10:24] Tom (ML Eng): we'll prep 3 payload profiles: short-interactive, long-historical (40k), and transcript-aggregate.
[10:31] Marisol (SE): perfect — while we're here a few gotchas I want to call out: 1) avoid single huge prompt appends — prefer compact references, 2) keep client retry jittered and honor Retry-After, 3) use the SDK resume tokens for streaming.
[10:45] Evan (SRE): noted. Also, any recommendations around nginx keepalive settings?
[10:51] Marisol (SE): set keepalive timeout > client timeout, increase proxy_buffer_size for large chunks, and disable proxy_request_buffering for streaming endpoints. We'll drop a config snippet.
[10:59] Aisha (CTO): any known issues with TLS termination and long-lived streams? we've had proxies terminate early if they thought traffic idle.
[11:07] Marisol (SE): that's usually due to idle detection; set idle timeout high and send small heartbeats every 15–30s. SDK does that automatically if enabled.
[11:18] Tom (ML Eng): final quick question — when you scale up burst lanes, is there a cold start penalty for model loading?
[11:26] Marisol (SE): yes model load can be 10–90s depending on size; warm pools and model prefetching mitigate this. Dedicated customers often keep a hot standby for peak windows.
[11:36] Liam (AE): okay we're getting near time — quick recap: Redwood will run the pilot once Nimbus shares prompts and TPS shapes; Marisol will send Optimize profile suggestions and the SDK streaming config; Liam will send security docs and pricing.
[11:49] Aisha (CTO): thanks, let's reconvene after pilot results.
[11:53] Liam (AE): thanks everyone, we'll follow up with calendar invites for the SRE deep-dive.

Notes about transcript quality: multiple speakers overlapped, occasional mis-heard words (e.g., 'K V cache' instead of 'KV cache'), timestamps approximate.

End of meeting.
